Last Tuesday at 4:47pm my GI specialist used the word "permanent" and slid a one-page printout across his desk. The printout was a study from 2024. The study said women on GLP-1 medication longer than 18 months had measurably slowed gastric emptying that did not return to baseline 6 months after they stopped the shot. I am 16 months in. I drove home from his office crying so hard I had to pull over twice.

I am 62 years old. I have lost 51 pounds on Mounjaro. I have a husband, two daughters, three grandchildren, and a printout from a gastroenterologist in my kitchen drawer that has been keeping me up at 3am for 8 nights in a row.

I'd like to back up.

I went on Mounjaro in January of last year. The shot did everything they said it would do. I lost 14 pounds the first month. The food noise that had been the soundtrack of my entire adult life went quiet for the first time since 1981. I stopped opening the refrigerator at 9pm just to look. I bought clothes I had not worn in 13 years. My husband told me at the bathroom mirror one Saturday morning that he could see the woman he married coming back. I cried in his bathrobe.

That is what the shot does. The shot fixes a thing nobody had been able to fix for me in 4 decades.

The shot also did something else.

By month 4 I was bloated by dinner. By month 7 I was going every fourth day. By month 11 I was sitting in my husband's recliner at 3am with a heating pad pressed against my upper ribs because the brick in my stomach would not let me lie flat.

I did what every woman on this shot does. I added a Miralax. Then a Metamucil. Then a magnesium. Then a probiotic the woman at the pharmacy promised me would change my life. Then a fiber gummy. Then a senna at bedtime when nothing else worked.

By month 14 I had a wire shelving unit installed in my bathroom cabinet just to organize the bottles. None of them were working. Not "less" working. Not "sometimes" working. Not working.

What finally made me call the GI specialist was something my younger daughter said on the phone in March. She was telling me about a colleague at her firm whose mother had quit Ozempic 11 months ago and was still constipated. Still bloated. Still going every fifth day. The colleague's mother had been told by her doctor that her gastric emptying might not return to normal. That she might be like this for the rest of her life. That she should have stopped the shot a year earlier.

My daughter said it casually. She did not know the bathroom cabinet I had built. She did not know the wire shelves. She did not know I had spent the last 8 months hiding the bottles from her father and lying to him about whether I had eaten dinner.

I drove to my primary care doctor that week and she referred me to a GI specialist. Dr. Levin. The first appointment available was three weeks out. I waited three weeks while my brain ran the math. 16 months. 16 months. 16 months. And the colleague's mother had only been on it for 14.

Last Tuesday at 4:47pm I sat across from Dr. Levin's desk in a chair that smelled like industrial carpet cleaner. He listened to me describe everything. The bottles. The recliner. The 4-day stretches. The lying to my husband at the dinner table. The recital I had cancelled in April. The wedding I had skipped in June. The fact that I had not slept a full night in 11 months because I had been lying awake doing math.

Then he opened a folder on his desk and slid a one-page printout across to me.

I read it twice.

The study was from 2024. It tracked 1,200 women over 50 who had been on a GLP-1 medication longer than 18 months. Six months after they discontinued the shot, more than half of them still had measurably slowed gastric emptying. A subset had not returned to baseline at 12 months. A smaller subset had not returned at 24.

The clinical term Dr. Levin used was "post-treatment gastroparesis."

He was very kind about it. He told me that the longer I stayed on the medication, the higher my odds of joining that subset. He told me he had three patients in his practice right now who had quit a GLP-1 over a year ago and still could not eat a normal dinner. He told me one of them was 58.

Then he said the sentence that has been keeping me up at 3am for 8 nights.

"Joan. You have a 60 to 90 day window where this is still likely reversible. After that, I cannot give you that promise."

I drove home crying. I pulled over twice. The first time was at the gas station on Route 9. The second time was in the parking lot of the Trader Joe's where I had cried 14 months earlier when the food noise stopped for the first time. I sat in my car in that same parking spot and I tried to figure out how a medication that had given me back my body could also be the medication that was about to take my stomach.

I called my older daughter that night. She is the accountant. She is the one who, when something is broken, will sit at a kitchen table for 6 hours figuring out what to do about it.

I told her about the printout. I told her about the 60 to 90 day window. I told her I could not afford to quit the shot because the food noise would come back and my marriage and my body and my whole life would unravel. And I could not afford to stay on the shot because Dr. Levin had used the word "permanent."

She was very quiet on the other end of the line. Then she said, "Mom, what if the answer is not quit or stay. What if the answer is to stop the actual mechanism that is causing the damage."

I did not know what she meant.

I want you to picture your stomach as a kitchen sink.

Not a colon. Not "your gut." A kitchen sink with a drain at the bottom that empties into the rest of the plumbing.

When the drain works, you can rinse anything down. Coffee grounds, last night's pasta water, the scraps off the dinner plates. It all goes down. The sink stays clean.

GLP-1 medication does one thing extraordinarily well. It half-clogs the drain.

That is in fact the point of the medication. It slows your stomach so food sits there longer and you feel full longer and you eat less. The slowdown is the medication doing its job. That is why the shot works.

But here is the part Dr. Levin showed me on the printout.

When you keep that drain half-clogged for long enough, the smooth muscle in the stomach wall stops remembering how to contract on its own. The pacemaker that runs the contraction rhythm — the one that has been firing 3 times per minute since you were a fetus — starts to atrophy. The longer it does not have to fire, the less it remembers how. By month 18 in some women, by month 24 in others, the pacemaker has been suppressed for so long that it cannot reliably restart even after the medication clears your system.

The slowed stomach becomes a permanently slow stomach. Not because the drug is still in you. Because the muscle has forgotten the rhythm.

That is what the printout was telling me. That is what Dr. Levin used the word "permanent" for. That is what the colleague's mother on Ozempic was living with 11 months after she quit.

And every single thing on my bathroom shelf, the Miralax, the Metamucil, the magnesium, the prune juice, the senna, the probiotics, was pointed at my colon.

The colon is six feet downstream of the stomach.

The damage was happening upstream.

Pouring drain cleaner into the bathtub does nothing for a clog in the kitchen sink. And it does nothing for the muscle in the kitchen sink that is forgetting how to push water down the drain.

That, in one sentence, is what makes this medication different from every gastrointestinal problem the laxative aisle was built for.

The clog is not the issue.

The muscle that should be doing the unclogging is going to sleep.

But here is what most women on the shot do not believe me when I tell them.

The pacemaker can be reminded.

The atrophy is not a death sentence. It is a use-it-or-lose-it situation. If the smooth muscle in your stomach wall is given the right signal at the right depth at the right window of time, it can re-engage. The studies on this go back decades. They were done on patients with diabetic gastroparesis long before anyone knew what a GLP-1 was.

There are three plant compounds with research behind them that work upstream, at the stomach, at the exact place the medication is suppressing motility.

Three compounds my GP had never mentioned. Three compounds the woman at the pharmacy had never mentioned. Three compounds that are not in a single bottle on the laxative aisle of any store I had been buying from for 14 months.

The first one is called apigenin. It is a flavonoid concentrated in celery juice extract and chamomile. The research on it goes back decades. Apigenin works on the smooth muscle in the stomach wall. It helps the stomach remember how to contract on its own. It does not override the medication. It does not force urgency the way a laxative does. It works at the on-ramp where the slowdown is, instead of the off-ramp where the laxatives have been firing.

The second is chlorophyllin. The stabilized form of the green pigment in plants. It binds the sulfur compounds and methane your gut bacteria are producing while the food sits there fermenting. It does not mask the smell. It deactivates the molecules the smell is made of. The fermentation byproducts that have been crawling up your esophagus stop reaching your throat because the molecules have already been deactivated.

The third is a soluble prebiotic fiber. Completely different from the bulking psyllium fiber the pharmacy keeps pushing on women like me. Bulking fiber adds mass to a stomach that cannot move what is already there. Soluble prebiotic fiber softens the food bolus while it is still in the stomach so the contractions, when they come back, have something soft to push.

Wake the stomach. Clear the ferment. Move the chain.

All three aiming at the upstream organ. None of them at the colon.

Six feet up from where the laxatives have been pointing for 14 months. And exactly where the muscle has been quietly atrophying for the same 14 months.

That is why I take Motilli.

It is the only product I have found that has all three compounds in the doses the research called for.

I want to be very honest about this because I do not want anyone reading this thinking I am sponsored or that I get paid every time someone clicks something. I have told my story so many times in the last 6 weeks at book club, at my hairdresser, at the GI specialist's waiting room when I went back for my follow-up, that my daughter said I should write it all down so I could just send it to people.

Motilli is a small company. They make a heart-shaped gummy. Two a day.

Apigenin from standardized celery extract, not powder, because powder loses the active compound on the shelf. Chlorophyllin in the stabilized form. A soluble prebiotic fiber, not psyllium, not bulk filler.

Most apigenin products on the shelf use ground-up celery powder at one-twentieth of the dose the studies used. Most chlorophyll products are sold for body odor. Most fiber products stack soluble fiber on top of psyllium and call it gut support.

Motilli does not. That is the whole reason it works.

I started the gummies on a Monday morning, 8 days after Dr. Levin slid the printout across his desk.

By Friday morning of that first week the sulfur burps stopped. Just stopped. I had not gone 4 days without one in 11 months.

Week 2 the bloat dropped two pant sizes. Not from more weight loss. From standing-water bloat that finally drained.

Week 3 I woke up at 6am on a Tuesday and I went. On my own. No senna. No magnesium the night before. I just got out of bed and went. I sat there for a full minute afterward because I genuinely could not remember the last time my body had done that without me forcing it.

Week 4 I went back to Dr. Levin for my follow-up. He pushed on my upper abdomen the way GI specialists do. He listened with the stethoscope. He frowned, then he stopped frowning. He told me the distension was visibly reduced and asked me what I had changed.

I told him about Motilli. He wrote the name down.

Then he said something that made me cry in his office for the second time in 5 weeks. He said, "Joan, if this is repeatable, you may have caught the window."

The window. The 60 to 90 day window where the muscle can still remember.

I have been on Motilli for 6 weeks. I am still on Mounjaro. I am still losing weight. The bloat is gone. The sulfur burps are gone. The recliner has been pushed back into the corner of the living room because I have not needed it at 3am in 41 nights.

I am not a doctor and I am not telling you what to do with your body. What I can tell you is what worked for me when a gastroenterologist used the word "permanent" and gave me a 60 to 90 day window I almost did not catch in time.

If you are sitting at your own kitchen table right now and you are 12, 14, 16, 18 months into Mounjaro or Wegovy or Ozempic and you have a wire shelf full of products that have not worked and a brick in your upper ribs by every dinner and a number in the back of your head you are afraid to say out loud, I hear you.

I sat in that same chair. I drove home from that same parking lot. I lay awake at 3am running the same math.

There are two versions of the next 90 days for you.

In one of them, you keep buying products designed for a colon that was never the problem. The clog in the kitchen sink stays clogged. The muscle in the stomach wall keeps quietly atrophying for another 90 days. You go from 16 months to 19 months on the shot, from 18 to 21, from 20 to 23. Each month the window Dr. Levin gave me for re-engagement gets a little narrower. The colleague's mother on Ozempic was on it for 14 months. She is now 11 months past her last dose and still bloated and still going every fifth day. There is a version of the next 90 days where you become her.

In the other one, you stop pointing drain cleaner at the wrong room. You aim two heart-shaped gummies at the upstream organ where the muscle is going to sleep. You give the pacemaker the signal it has been waiting for. And you watch what happens between week 1 and week 6 to a body that, like mine, has been begging for the right intervention.

That is the whole choice.

Motilli is the only thing I have found that aims at the kitchen sink.

I am not affiliated with the company. I do not get paid when someone clicks a link. I am writing this because Dr. Levin's printout almost got to me too late, and the women I have met in his waiting room since then have made it clear that I am not the only one who is running out of window.

Motilli runs a 90 day money back guarantee. If the bloat does not drop, if the burps do not stop, if your bathroom mornings do not start coming back, you email them and they refund the card. You keep the bottle. In 14 months of buying constipation products at three different drugstores I never saw a single bottle that came with a guarantee like that. The closest any of them came was a "no returns on opened bottles" sticker on the back of the box. Every other product I tried was certain enough that it would not work that they refused to take it back. Motilli has staked the entire 90 days on the only outcome that matters.

Motilli is a small company. They batch-produce the gummies because the apigenin in standardized celery extract starts losing strength once it sits on a shelf for too long. That is exactly why most apigenin products on the shelf do nothing. They have been sitting in a warehouse for 8 months before they reach you. Motilli does not keep months of inventory. They make small runs to keep the active compound live, which means they sell out for stretches at a time, especially as more women on GLP-1 medication find them through their daughters and their book clubs and their GI waiting rooms the way I did. The week I ordered, the page was within days of going dark. If you have a 60 to 90 day window the way Dr. Levin told me I had, do not wait until next Wednesday. Check availability tonight.

👉 https://getmotilli.com

You still have time. I almost did not. I am 62 years old and I caught my window with about 3 weeks to spare. You have not lost yours yet.

---

P.S. If you have read this far, you already know.

You know the printout you have not looked up because you are afraid of what the study will say. You know the GI appointment you keep rescheduling. You know the number of months you have been on the shot that you have stopped saying out loud, even to your husband.

You did not need a stranger on the internet to tell you any of that.

What you needed was someone to tell you that the window is real and the window is closing and the window is not closed yet.

There is a gummy that aims at the muscle that is going to sleep. There is a 90 day promise that says you do not pay if it does not work. There is a small company that batch-makes the thing because the active compound does not survive a warehouse.

The page is in stock as of this morning. It has been 41 nights since I last needed the recliner.

creative.title: GLP-1 Medication Does Not Slow Your Colon. It Slows Your Stomach. And After Month 18, The Damage May Not Reverse.
